title: Story Of King Shahryar and His Brother
full_text:
In the ancient kingdoms of the East, King Shahryar ruled over an empire stretching across Persia and India, while his younger brother, Shahzaman, governed the kingdom of Samarkand. Both monarchs were famed for their splendor and power, yet both suffered bitter disillusionment when betrayal struck their households. Stricken by deep melancholy and mistrust, Shahryar retreated to his capital, declaring in his wounded anger that faith and loyalty had vanished from humankind.

For a long time, the shadow of the sultan’s gloom lay heavy over the city. The grand palace grew quiet, the bazaars lost their song, and the vizier walked with bowed shoulders, weeping for his lord’s hardened soul. In that household dwelt the vizier’s elder daughter, Shahrazad, a maiden of extraordinary intellect, courage, and grace. She had read the chronicles of ancient kings, studied the traditions of past nations, mastered philosophy, medicine, and poetry, and stored in her memory more than a thousand volumes of wisdom.

Seeing her father’s grief, Shahrazad spoke with steady resolve: "O father, I beg of you, present me to King Shahryar. Either I shall perish in the attempt, or I shall heal his heart and deliver our people from this enduring sorrow." The vizier turned pale and warned her with parables of danger, yet Shahrazad’s heart remained unshakeable. "Fear not," she replied softly. "Wisdom is an armor that steel cannot pierce."

When she was brought before King Shahryar, she made one humble request: that her younger sister, Dunyazad, might sit by her feet until the hour of dawn. The king, struck by Shahrazad’s calm majesty, consented. As night fell over the palace and the oil lamps flickered against the arabesque tiles, Dunyazad murmured: "O sister, if you are not yet weary, recount to us one of your wonderful tales before morning breaks."

Shahrazad turned her luminous eyes toward the king and said: "With royal leave, O Commander of the Faithful, I shall gladly tell a story of wonder and truth." King Shahryar, expecting nothing more than a passing diversion, granted permission. Thus began the first of the Thousand and One Nights—a tapestry of cunning spirits, brave travelers, honest merchants, and enchanted gardens. As the first light of dawn tinted the minarets, Shahrazad paused at the height of suspense. The king, eager to know the fate of the travelers, spared her day after day. With every passing night, her stories sowed seeds of mercy, understanding, and justice, slowly restoring the monarch’s faith in humanity and bringing golden peace to the kingdom.
moral: Patience, wisdom, and the healing power of stories can soften the hardest of hearts and bring peace to an entire realm.

title: Tale of the Bull and the Ass
full_text:
In a fertile valley between the two great rivers lived a wealthy merchant endowed with a secret gift: he understood the speech of all beasts, birds, and creeping things. Yet this gift carried a strict warning—should he ever reveal to another human being what the creatures spoke, his peace of mind and very fortune would be forfeited.

In the merchant's courtyard stood a sturdy bull and a sleek, well-fed donkey. Each morning, the bull was harnessed to the heavy iron plow, driven through the rocky fields beneath the burning sun, and returned at dusk drenched in sweat and bruised by the yoke. The donkey, by contrast, spent his days resting beneath shaded palms, dining on sifted barley and clear fountain water, his only labor being to carry the master gently to market when occasion arose.

One evening, as the bull collapsed into the stable with weary groans, the donkey looked over with smug pity. "Friend," said the donkey, "why do you suffer so meekly? Tomorrow, when the plowman comes with your fodder, refuse to eat. Thrash the ground, moan as if struck by illness, and do not rise. If you pretend to be frail, the master will surely let you rest in the cool shade."

The bull thanked the donkey for his ingenious counsel. The next dawn, when the servant brought grain, the bull rolled his eyes, kicked his legs, and feigned dreadful weakness. The servant ran to the merchant in alarm. But the merchant, who had overheard the donkey's whispering the previous night, smiled knowingly. "Since the bull is too sick to plow," ordered the merchant, "harness the healthy donkey in his place and work him without mercy until sunset."

All through the scorching day, the pampered donkey was dragged through briars and mud, whipped whenever he faltered, and forced to turn the heavy earth. When dusk arrived, the donkey staggered back to the stall with broken knees, a bloody neck, and ribs trembling with agony. The bull looked up gratefully: "Blessings upon you, wise companion! Your advice brought me a day of sweet slumber."

The donkey coughed through dust and replied bitterly: "Hear my latest news, brother. As I labored, I overheard the merchant whisper to the butcher that if the bull does not stand strong tomorrow, he must be sold to the meat market." At once the bull leaped to his feet, devoured all his straw, and vowed to pull the plow with double vigor. The merchant, listening behind the partition, laughed heartily at how the meddlesome donkey had cured his own pride by tasting the bitter fruit of his own scheming.
moral: He who meddles unwisely in another's burden may find himself forced to carry it all on his own shoulders.

title: Tale of the Merchant and His Wife
full_text:
The merchant who understood the language of animals lived happily in a countryside manor surrounded by gardens, flocks, and poultry. One starlit evening, as he sat upon the terrace beside his wife, a mother goat passed with her playful kid. The kid leaped into the air and tumbled into the irrigation channel. From the roost nearby, a venerable rooster crowed a witty observation to the farm dog about how young creatures test their boundaries before discovering their balance.

Hearing the bird's clever remark, the merchant could not restrain himself and burst into loud, merry laughter. His wife immediately turned to him with suspicious eyes and asked: "At what are you laughing with such delight? Are you mocking me in secret?"

The merchant smiled gently and placed his hand upon his chest. "By my honor, dear wife, my amusement was born of the barnyard banter which I alone can interpret. It touches you in no way whatsoever." Yet the wife, consumed by curiosity and wounded pride, refused to believe him. "You must tell me exactly what you heard," she insisted. "If you hide your secrets from me, it means your heart is no longer mine."

"Wife," pleaded the merchant, "I cannot disclose it! The covenant of my gift decrees that if I reveal what the beasts speak, my vitality and prosperity will perish." Still, she wept, locked herself in her chambers, and gathered her kinsmen, vowing to neither eat nor drink until the secret was laid bare. Torn between his love for her and the peril of his vow, the merchant sat in despair, preparing his will.

As he walked sorrowfully through the yard, he noticed the proud rooster strutting among the hens, pecking grains and crowing with supreme authority. The farm dog barked in annoyance: "How can you strut and rejoice when our master is preparing for his demise over his wife’s obstinacy?" The rooster shook his scarlet comb and answered: "Our master may be wise in languages, but he lacks resolve! A man must not surrender his life and judgment to petulant whim. A firm word, an unyielding boundary, and an olive branch of reason are the true remedies for domestic peace."

Hearing this, the merchant felt a veil lift from his eyes. He gathered his courage, entered his wife's presence with quiet authority, and told her plainly that her demands were unjust and that no whim would make him destroy their family. Seeing his unwavering resolve and dignity, the wife realized the folly of her relentless pressure. She cast aside her obstinacy, embraced him with newfound reverence, and domestic harmony returned to the manor forever.
moral: True household leadership requires firmness, calm discernment, and mutual respect, rather than yielding to endless unreasonable demands.

title: Tale of the Trader and the Jinn
full_text:
There was once a prosperous merchant of Baghdad who possessed great wealth, vast estates, and an unblemished reputation for honesty. One summer, having debts to collect in a distant province, he mounted his horse, filled his saddlebags with dried dates, biscuits, and a flask of cool water, and set forth across the dusty plains.

Having accomplished his business successfully, he turned homeward. On the fourth day, beneath the blazing midday sun, he sought refuge under the spreading boughs of a wild walnut tree near a bubbling spring. He tethered his steed, opened his wallet, and began to eat sweet dates, tossing the hard stones casually across his shoulder. Suddenly, the earth trembled. A dense column of smoke billowed from the sand, twisting into the towering form of an enormous Jinni, whose eyes glowed like coals and who brandished a naked scimitar of blue steel.

"Arise, O wretched mortal!" roared the spirit in a voice of thunder. "I must slay you even as you have slain my son!" The merchant trembled with amazement and cried: "How could a frail creature like me slay a child of the unseen?" The Jinni answered wrathfully: "When you cast away your date stones without warning, one struck my invisible son in the breast, and he expired on the instant. Blood demands blood!"

The merchant fell upon his knees and wept bitterly: "I had no malice, O mighty spirit! Spare my life, for I have a loving wife, young children, and debts of honor yet unpaid." Seeing the Jinni unmoved, the merchant made a noble plea: "Grant me a reprieve of one single year. By the Creator of the heavens, I swear to return to this very tree on the anniversary of this day, that you may execute your judgment upon me. Let me but divide my inheritance, provide for my family, and discharge every coin I owe to my creditors."

The Jinni, astonished by the man's solemn oath and steadfast character, bound him to the covenant and vanished into the earth. The merchant returned home, fulfilled all his obligations, embraced his weeping family with tearful farewells, and when the year drew to its close, put on his shroud and rode back to the walnut tree, choosing death with honor over life bought by broken faith.
moral: Honesty and keeping one's sacred word in the face of death inspire mercy and invoke the highest virtues in others.

title: The First Shaykh's Story
full_text:
As the merchant sat under the walnut tree waiting for the Jinni to claim his life, an elderly shaykh approached, leading a graceful gazelle by a silken cord. Seeing the traveler weeping in a shroud, the old man asked the reason for his sorrow. When the merchant recounted his oath to the Jinni, the shaykh marveled at his steadfast honor and said: "By heavens, I shall not depart until I behold the outcome of this extraordinary deed."

Presently, the earth opened with a roar of wind, and the monstrous Jinni appeared with raised blade, ready to strike down the merchant. The first shaykh stepped forward, kissed the spirit's hand, and said: "O lord of spirits, if I recount to you the history of myself and this gazelle, and you find it more wondrous than this man’s plight, will you remit one-third of his blood-debt unto me?" The Jinni paused and replied: "Speak, old man; if your tale is truly wonderful, I shall grant your request."

The shaykh began: "Know, O spirit, that this gazelle was once my cousin and wife of thirty years. Having no children by her, I took a maid into my household who bore me a son as fair as the crescent moon. When the boy reached twelve years of age, I embarked on a long trading journey. While I was absent, my wife, consumed by bitter jealousy and skilled in dark sorcery, transformed my son into a yearling calf and his mother into a cow, giving them to my herdsman to be slaughtered.

When I returned, heart-broken by their supposed disappearance, the feast of sacrifice arrived. The herdsman brought forth the cow, but as I raised the blade, she lowed with such agonizing sorrow that my soul recoiled. I spared her and commanded the calf to be brought. The young creature ran to me, rubbed his head against my garments, and wept human tears. My heart melted; I stayed my hand and gave the calf back to the herdsman’s care.

Soon after, the herdsman’s daughter, who was learned in the pure arts of counter-magic, recognized the enchantment upon my kin. She broke the spell, restored my son to his princely form, and bound my spiteful wife into the form of this silent gazelle. Yet despite her past betrayal, I nourish her with tender hands and guide her with silk, repaying hatred with mercy."

The Jinni marveled at the tale, shook his massive head, and said: "This is indeed a wonder of wonders. I remit one-third of the merchant’s blood unto you."
moral: Envy and cruelty wither the soul, while fidelity and gentle compassion undo the darkest enchantments.

title: The Second Shaykh's Story
full_text:
Before the Jinni could raise his blade again, a second venerable shaykh approached leading two sleek black hounds upon a leash. Learning of the merchant's covenant and having witnessed the first third of the pardon granted, the newcomer bowed before the Jinni and said: "O sovereign spirit, if my tale of these two hounds surpasses even the wonder you have just heard, will you remit another third of this noble merchant's punishment?" The Jinni answered: "Tell your tale, O traveler."

The second shaykh spoke: "These two hounds are not beasts by birth, but my own elder brothers. When our father died, he left us three thousand gold dinars, which we divided equally. Each opened a shop in the market. Soon, my brothers sold their goods and resolved to travel foreign lands with caravans. I warned them of distant perils, but they departed. After a year, both returned in rags, having squandered everything in reckless ventures. Instead of reproaching them, I embraced them, took them into my home, and divided my own earnings to set them up anew.

Again they sought adventure, and again they returned destitute. A third time I opened my coffers and restored their dignity. Thereafter, we agreed to buy a ship and sail together for sea-trade. In an uncharted port, I wed a poor, pious maiden who asked for nothing but my kindness. My brothers, observing my prosperous cargo and fortunate marriage, allowed toxic jealousy to fester within their chests. One midnight, while our ship plowed the deep sea, they seized my sleeping bride and me and cast us into the dark waves.

Unknown to them, my wife was a benevolent spirit of the ocean. She summoned dolphins that carried us safely to a sunlit shore. Transporting me back to my native city, she revealed that my treacherous brothers had been spared drowning only to face judgment. She transformed them into these two mute hounds, commanding that they remain bound to my side for ten years. Yet look upon them, O Jinni—though they sought my destruction, I feed them from my own dish and wash them with my own hands, praying daily for their redemption."

The Jinni was deeply moved by such boundless fraternal forgiveness. He clapped his hands in wonder and proclaimed: "I grant you the second third of the man's life!"
moral: Generosity and endless forgiveness toward kin reveal noble breeding, whereas treacherous jealousy consumes its own master.

title: The Third Shaykh's Story
full_text:
Now only one-third of the merchant's life remained forfeit, and the Jinni stood waiting, his fiery visage softened by curiosity. Then stepped forward the third traveler, leading a dappled mule whose eyes gleamed with unnatural sorrow. "O Commander of the Unseen," said the traveler, "grant me leave to tell the story of this mule. If my history matches the strange wonders of the others, grant this righteous merchant complete freedom." The Jinni nodded: "Let me hear your words."

The third shaykh said: "Know, O spirit, that this mule was once a haughty sorcerer who held sway over a mountain village. He demanded tribute from the honest weavers and shepherds, turning into stone anyone who spoke the plain truth. I was then a simple traveler wandering through his territory, carrying nothing but a staff and a pouch of medicinal herbs.

When I entered the square and saw the villagers weeping under his oppressive spells, I challenged him before his council. He mocked my poverty and cast a curse of burning coals at my feet. But because my heart held no greed or fear, the coals turned to cool rose petals beneath my sandals. Surprised and enraged, he transformed into a roaring leopard to tear me apart. With swift presence of mind, I scattered water from the sacred well of the village and spoke the ancient words of truth that strip all impostors of their illusions.

The sorcerer was trapped by his own pride and condensed into the form of this humble mule. The villagers wished to cast him off a precipice, but I forbade them, saying: 'Vengeance only breeds another cycle of bitterness. Let him carry the packs of the weary across the mountain paths until labor purifies his arrogant mind.' For seven long years he has carried wheat and water for the poor, learning the weight of honest toil."

The Jinni listened with wide eyes, marveling at how wisdom had conquered black magic without shedding a single drop of blood. He sheathed his scimitar, bowed to the three shaykhs, and embraced the honest merchant. "Your debt is paid in full," declared the Jinni. "Go in peace to your wife and children, for your steadfast truthfulness has gathered around you the most wonderful friends in all creation." Thus the merchant returned home in joy, praising the power of honor and the marvels of the world.
moral: Truth, humility, and steadfast courage can undo the deepest malice and soften the harshest decrees of fate.

title: The Fisherman and the Jinni
full_text:
On the rocky coast of a blue sea lived an aged fisherman who supported a wife and three small children by casting his nets four times each day. One morning, he cast his net and pulled with heavy labor, only to find a dead donkey tangled in the ropes. He cast a second time, and dragged up an earthen jar filled with mud and stones. On his third attempt, he recovered only broken pots and useless seaweed.

Lifting his hands to the heavens, the fisherman prayed for sustenance and cast his net for the fourth and final time. When he drew the cords, the weight was immense. Dragging it ashore, he discovered a heavy flask of yellow copper, sealed tight with lead bearing the sacred seal-ring of King Solomon. Overjoyed, he thought: "I shall sell this fine brass vessel in the foundry for ten gold dinars!"

Curious to see what lay inside, he took his small knife, loosened the lead seal, and shook the jar. At first, nothing emerged. Then, a thin plume of blue smoke curled out of the neck, rising higher and higher into the clouds until it spanned the sky like a thunderhead. The smoke condensed, shook itself, and transformed into a monstrous Jinni whose head brushed the clouds, whose nostrils were like caves, and whose fiery eyes flashed with terrifying wrath.

Seeing the tiny fisherman trembling on the sand, the giant roared: "Rejoice, O fisherman, for you shall die this very hour!" The fisherman cried: "Why should you slay me when I have delivered you from the depths of the sea?" The Jinni answered: "For the first hundred years of my imprisonment, I vowed to enrich whoever freed me forever. For the second century, I vowed to open all the treasures of the earth. But by the fourth century, my fury grew so vast that I swore an oath to grant my deliverer only the choice of how he wishes to be slain!"

The fisherman's wits sharpened in the face of imminent doom. "If I must die," said the fisherman meekly, "answer me one true question. By the seal of Solomon that held you, how could a giant whose head reaches the clouds ever have fitted inside a vessel scarcely large enough for a newborn lamb? My eyes refuse to believe it."

"Do you doubt my power, wretched insect?" bellowed the Jinni. Instantly, the spirit dissolved himself back into a winding stream of smoke and poured himself down through the narrow neck of the jar until the last wisp disappeared inside. Quick as lightning, the fisherman slapped the lead seal back into place and rolled the heavy jar to the edge of the cliff. The trapped Jinni wailed from within, but the fisherman laughed: "Stay there until the end of time, unless you swear never to harm me and to lead me to true fortune!"
moral: Wit and clever presence of mind can outmatch sheer physical might and arrogant fury.

title: Tale of the Wazir and the Sage Duban
full_text:
As the Jinni pleaded from within the sealed copper jar, the fisherman spoke from the cliff: "Listen, O spirit, to the history of King Yunan and the sage Duban, that you may understand how ingratitude brings swift ruin upon those who repay kindness with malice."

In ancient Persia, King Yunan was afflicted with an incurable leprosy that baffled all the royal doctors and astrologers. One day, a foreign sage named Duban arrived at court. He was deeply versed in Greek, Persian, and Arabic sciences, possessing profound knowledge of medicinal herbs and planetary motions. Approaching the throne, Duban said: "O King, I shall cure your affliction without draughts to swallow or ointments to smear upon your flesh."

The king was incredulous, but Duban prepared a hollow polo mallet filled with secret herbs and aromatic essences. He instructed the monarch to ride out onto the field, strike the ball until his brow perspired, and then retire to the bath. As the king played, the warmth of his hands drew the potent vapors through the handle into his veins. When Yunan emerged from the bath the next morning, his skin was as smooth, pure, and clear as virgin silver.

Overjoyed, the king clothed Duban in robes of gold, seated him beside his throne, and bestowed upon him vast estates. Yet this sudden favor ignited poisonous envy in the breast of the king's chief vizier. Creeping to the throne, the vizier whispered: "Sire, this physician is an assassin in disguise. He who could cure you from a distance without touching you can just as easily take your life with a poisoned flower!"

King Yunan hesitated, poisoned by suspicion. Despite Duban's tears and pleas for justice, the king condemned the innocent physician to the scaffold. Before the sword fell, Duban asked only that his magical volume, the Book of Wonders, be presented to the king after his demise. When the monarch opened the book and found the parchment pages stuck together, he repeatedly moistened his fingers with his tongue to turn the leaves. The pages were steeped in swift poison, and within an hour the ungrateful king perished, reaping the bitter harvest of his betrayal.
moral: He who digs a pit of jealousy for the innocent shall ultimately fall into it himself.

title: Story of King Sindibad and His Falcon
full_text:
To illustrate the folly of hasty anger, the vizier of King Yunan had related an even older tale concerning King Sindibad of Persia, a monarch renowned for his passion for the hunt. Among all his hounds and hawks, his favorite was a noble falcon that wore a golden bell and never left his wrist, trained with such perfection that it never failed to strike its prey.

One scorching summer day, the king pursued an antelope far into the wilderness, outstripping all his courtiers. The heat was fierce, and his throat burned with unbearable thirst. Riding along the foot of a barren rocky ridge, he noticed thick drops of moisture dripping slowly from the crevice of an overhanging rock. Believing it to be a trickle of clear mountain spring water, the king took a crystal cup from his saddlebag and held it beneath the rock until it filled to the brim.

Just as he raised the cup to his parched lips, the falcon leaped from his wrist, beat its wings furiously, and overturned the vessel, spilling the liquid upon the burning sands. The king frowned, thinking the bird was merely impatient. He reprimanded the hawk, placed the cup beneath the cliff once more, and waited patiently as it filled drop by drop. When he raised it a second time, the falcon again struck the cup with its talons, sending it crashing to the earth.

Consumed by blinding rage and maddened by thirst, King Sindibad drew his hunting dagger and struck the falcon, severing its wings. The dying bird fluttered weakly, lifted its head toward the summit of the rock, and pointed with its beak. The king climbed the rocky ledge to find the source of the water. To his absolute horror, he discovered a monstrous viper sleeping within the crevice, and the liquid dripping down the stone was not water, but deadly venom oozing from the serpent's fangs.

The king stood frozen, his heart pierced with agonizing remorse. His faithful falcon had perceived the poison and risked its life to save its master. Weeping bitter tears of shame, Sindibad carried the lifeless bird back to his palace and gave it a royal burial, forever mourning the hasty temper that had slain his truest protector.
moral: Never act in blind wrath, lest you destroy the very friend who sacrificed everything to save your life.

title: Tale of the Husband and the Parrot
full_text:
In a bustling quarter of Baghdad lived a wealthy merchant who owned a rare and articulate parrot, gifted with such extraordinary intelligence that it could repeat everything spoken in its presence and describe every visitor who crossed the threshold. Because the merchant traveled frequently on business, he placed the bird in a gilded cage in his courtyard to guard his domestic peace.

One day, returning from a three-day journey, the merchant questioned the bird. The parrot truthfully recounted that while he was away, an unwanted visitor had entered the house and eaten his sweetmeats. Enraged, the merchant confronted his household and demanded an explanation. His wife, realizing that the feathered observer had reported the matter, resolved to silence its credibility through clever deception.

The following night, when the merchant was again absent, the wife ordered her maidservant to turn an olive mill beneath the parrot's cage, while another servant poured water through a sieve above it, and a third waved a polished mirror reflecting candlelight across the ceiling. All night long, the bird was drenched with spray, deafened by rumbling stones, and blinded by artificial lightning, believing that a ferocious tempest had engulfed the city.

When the master returned at dawn, he asked the parrot: "What news have you of last night?" The parrot shivered and answered: "O master, ask me nothing! The heavens opened with thunder, lightning struck the courtyard, and rain poured in such torrents that I feared I should drown in my cage!"

The merchant stepped outside into the courtyard and saw the dust dry as powder, the sky cloudless, and the neighbors enjoying the tranquil morning. Believing that the parrot was a compulsive liar that had invented tales of falsehood against his family, the merchant flew into a temper, seized the cage, and dashed the poor bird against the pavement. Only later, when the maid confessed the trick, did the merchant learn that the parrot had spoken nothing but the truth, leaving the merchant to weep inconsolably over his hasty, tragic folly.
moral: Hasty judgment based on deceptive appearances destroys trust and leaves a lifetime of sorrow.

title: Tale of the Prince and the Ogress
full_text:
There was once a young prince who was the pride of his father's court, but his father's chief counselor was secretly an indolent man who neglected his duties. One day, the prince rode out into the desert on a spirited stallion, accompanied only by this counselor. As they galloped across the dunes, a magnificent wild gazelle crossed their path. The prince shouted to his guardian to join the chase, but the sluggish counselor stayed behind and let the prince ride alone into the trackless wilderness.

After riding for hours, the prince lost both the gazelle and his bearings. As twilight descended, he came upon the ruins of a fortress beside an ancient well. Sitting upon a crumbling wall was a young damsel clothed in silken robes, weeping bitterly. Moved by compassion, the prince dismounted and asked: "Who are you, fair maiden, and what has brought you to this desolate wasteland?"

The damsel sighed and answered: "I am the daughter of a king of India. While traveling with my caravan, sleep overcame me upon my camel, and I tumbled onto the sands. The caravan passed on, leaving me helpless and alone." Hearing her plight, the chivalrous prince lifted her onto his horse behind his saddle and set off toward the distant city lights.

As they rode past an ancient burial ground, the damsel asked to dismount for a moment behind a ruined wall. The prince waited, but hearing strange guttural voices, he crept softly to a chink in the stones. To his horror, he saw the maiden had transformed into a monstrous ogress, whispering to her ravenous brood: "Rejoice, my children! I have brought you a tender young prince on a fat stallion!"

The prince's blood ran cold, but he mastered his terror. Creeping back to his steed, he mounted silently and lifted his hands to the heavens, reciting words of divine protection and seeking refuge from deceit. The ogress returned, resuming her lovely disguise, and asked: "Why are you trembling, young rider?" The prince answered: "I am praying to the Protector of the innocent, who delivers the righteous from treacherous snares!" Sensing his awakened wisdom and seeing his hand grip his blade, the ogress shrieked in defeat and vanished like smoke into the tomb, leaving the prince to gallop safely home to his thankful father.
moral: In moments of mortal danger, humble prayer and calm clarity deliver the soul from the most cunning snares.

title: Tale of the Ensorcelled Prince
full_text:
When the fisherman convinced the Jinni to grant him true fortune, the spirit led him to an isolated valley nestled between four mysterious hills. In the center lay a shimmering lake whose waters teemed with fish of four distinct colors: white, red, blue, and yellow. The Jinni commanded the fisherman to cast his net once, take the catch to the Sultan of the city, and never fish there more than once a day.

The fisherman caught four magnificent fish and presented them to the Sultan, who rewarded him with four hundred pieces of gold. But when the royal cook placed the fish into a copper frying pan, the wall of the kitchen opened, and a maiden of supernatural beauty emerged, tapped the pan with a wand of bamboo, and overturned the fish into the coals before vanishing. Astounded, the Sultan resolved to uncover the secret of the four-colored fish himself.

Riding alone into the wilderness, the Sultan discovered a magnificent palace built of polished black marble, surrounded by silent gardens. Entering its deserted halls, he heard the faint sound of groaning. Following the voice, he drew back a tapestry and beheld a handsome young prince sitting upon a raised dais. When the Sultan bade him rise, the youth lifted his robe, revealing with tears that from his waist to his feet he was transformed into solid black stone.

The prince recounted his tragic history: he had been the rightful monarch of the Four Islands, but his treacherous queen, an adept in dark sorcery, had overthrown his throne, turned him half to stone, transformed his loyal citizens into fish of four colors according to their four original quarters, and turned his four majestic hills into an enchanted wilderness.

Moved to profound pity, the Sultan devised a daring plan. In the dead of night, he crept into the sorceress's secret pavilion, overpowered her champion, and disguised himself in the champion's garments. When the sorceress approached, the Sultan mimicked her confidant's voice and commanded her to break the enchantment upon the prince and the four islands before she could receive his favor. Deceived by love and fear, the sorceress sprinkled enchanted water, restoring the stone prince to flesh and blood, and transforming the lake back into a thriving, joyful city. The Sultan then struck down the sorceress, adopted the brave prince as his own son, and made the humble fisherman the chief treasurer of his realm.
moral: Perseverance against tyranny and cruelty will ultimately liberate the oppressed and restore stolen joy.

title: The Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad
full_text:
In the glorious days of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, there lived in Baghdad a bachelor porter of merry disposition and great physical strength. One morning, as he stood waiting in the public square with his woven basket, a tall lady wrapped in an embroidered silk veil approached him and said with a musical voice: "Take up your crate, O porter, and follow me."

The porter followed her eagerly through the fragrant souks. At the fruiterer's, she purchased Syrian apples, Ottoman quinces, Muscatel melons, and clusters of Egyptian limes. At the perfumer's, she bought rosewater, musk, ambergris, and aloes-wood. At the confectioner's, she loaded his basket with almond cakes, honey pastries, and pistachio pies. At last she halted before a grand mansion with a double door of bronze.

When the doors swung open, the porter was ushered into a courtyard of breathtaking splendor, with marble fountains, singing nightingales, and mosaic colonnades. There sat two other maidens of peerless beauty: the mistress of the mansion, Amine, and the gentle portress, Safie. The ladies paid the porter generously, but seeing his reluctance to depart from such enchanting company, they laughed at his merry wit and invited him to share their evening banquet.

"Stay with us, merry porter," said the eldest lady, "but under one strict condition: whatever you see, ask no questions concerning that which does not concern you, lest you hear what will not please you." The porter clapped his hands and bowed: "I swear by the hospitality of this roof to keep a silent tongue and an open heart!"

As the wine flowed and lutes were plucked, three wandering dervishes, each blind in the left eye and with shaven crowns, knocked at the portal seeking shelter. Soon after, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid himself, disguised as an ordinary merchant alongside his vizier Ja'afar and his executioner Masrur, entered seeking lodging from the night patrol. Within that single hall sat the greatest ruler on earth, three mysterious princes, three enchanting ladies, and a merry porter, all bound by the golden law of hospitality—until curiosity tested their vows.
moral: Courtesy, discretion, and respecting boundaries are the keys to true fellowship and good fortune.

title: The First Kalandar's Tale
full_text:
When the ladies of Baghdad demanded that their guests reveal their true histories on pain of banishment, the first one-eyed Kalandar stepped forward, placed his hand upon his breast, and began:

"Know, O noble company, that I was not born a mendicant dervish, but the son of a mighty king. From my youth, I was trained in horsemanship, jurisprudence, and warfare, while my cousin, the son of my father's brother, was my dearest companion. When my uncle died, my cousin inherited his kingdom, and I traveled to his court to celebrate his accession.

One evening, my cousin led me secretly to an ancient burial vault outside the city walls. Opening an iron trapdoor concealed beneath a slab of marble, he descended into a subterranean palace sumptuously furnished with silk tapestries and aromatic lamps. He turned to me with tears in his eyes and made me swear a sacred oath to seal the vault above him and reveal its secret to no living soul. Bound by love, I obeyed his desperate plea.

When I returned to my father's capital, a terrible catastrophe greeted me. My father's treacherous vizier had raised an army, murdered the king, and usurped the throne. I was seized and brought before the tyrant, who had long hated me because in childhood an arrow from my bow had accidentally struck him in the eye. In vengeance, he put out my left eye with a red-hot iron and ordered his guards to execute me in the desert.

The executioner, who had loved my father, took pity on me and bade me flee beyond the borders. I shaved my beard, donned the woollen cloak of a Kalandar, and wandered from kingdom to kingdom, learning that worldly crowns are as fragile as morning mist. Content with a crust of bread and a sip of clear water, I reached Baghdad this night, seeking nothing but peace."

The ladies wept at his misfortunes and granted him safety, while the Caliph whispered in astonishment at how royal blood walked humbly among the poor.
moral: Earthly splendor is fleeting; only inner humility and honor endure through the turns of destiny.

title: The Second Kalandar's Tale
full_text:
The second one-eyed Kalandar bowed before the company and said: "I too was born a prince, reared in science, philosophy, and the arts of poetry. When my father sent me with royal gifts to the Emperor of Hind, our caravan was attacked by fierce desert nomads. Alone and penniless, I escaped into an unknown kingdom, where I earned my bread as a woodcutter in a great forest.

One day, my axe struck an iron ring embedded in the earth. Lifting the ring, I discovered stairs leading down into a subterranean palace where an enchanted princess had been imprisoned by an evil Ifrit. For a time we shared delightful discourse, but the jealous demon returned, discovered my presence, and tore the palace asunder. To punish me, the Ifrit did not take my life, but transformed me by dark incantations into an ugly ape and cast me onto a desert island.

I wandered the shores until a trading vessel took pity on me. The sailors marveled that an ape ate with manners and observed human modesty. When we reached the capital of a great Sultan, the king's scribes had died, and the monarch had offered the office of grand vizier to whoever could write the most exquisite verses in six classic scripts. The sailors brought me to the palace as a curiosity. I seized the reed pen, dipped it in ink, and wrote poems of sublime wisdom in flawless calligraphy, alternating six styles of script.

The Sultan was astounded. He dressed me in silk robes, challenged me to chess—which I won three times with brilliant strategy—and treated me as his closest companion. Yet his royal daughter, a maiden instructed in divine sciences, recognized that the ape was a cursed prince. In a titanic battle of sorcery, the princess transformed into a falcon, a wolf, and a flame, destroying the Ifrit in the sky, though a stray spark struck my eye, leaving me blind on the left side. Restored to human form, I took the Kalandar's staff and journeyed to Baghdad to ponder the mysteries of fate."
moral: Intellect, learning, and eloquence can elevate a man even when cruel fate strips him of his human form.

title: Tale of the Envier and the Envied
full_text:
To illustrate the power of innocence over malice, the second Kalandar recounted a story he had learned during his travels:

In a tranquil town lived two neighbors. One was a man of boundless generosity, whose door was always open to the destitute and whose speech was sweet as honeycomb. The other was a bitter, resentful man whose chest burned with agony whenever he saw his neighbor prosper. Unable to bear his neighbor's good name, the envious man slandered him across the markets.

Realizing that his mere existence caused his neighbor misery, the good man sold his house, moved to a distant capital, and built a modest hermitage beside an ancient, dry well outside the city walls. There he lived as a holy ascetic, praying, tending a garden, and feeding travelers. Soon, people flocked from all directions to seek his blessing and counsel.

When news of the hermit's fame reached the envious man, his envy flared into murderous hatred. He traveled to the hermitage, embraced the hermit with feigned affection, and whispered: "Dear friend, I bring secret news of great import. Walk with me beside the ancient well." When they reached the lip of the pit, the envious man violently pushed his benefactor into the dark abyss and fled, confident that his rival was dead.

Now, the well was inhabited by benevolent spirits who caught the holy man gently in their arms and set him safely upon the sandy floor. As he sat in darkness, he overheard the spirits whispering above: "Know you who this righteous man is? And know you that the Sultan's daughter is afflicted with a mysterious malady that no doctor can cure? If the king but burns seven hairs from the tail of the black cat that sleeps in his stables, and perfumes the princess with the smoke, the affliction will leave her instantly!"

The hermit memorized the secret, climbed out of the well at dawn, and presented himself at the Sultan's palace. He applied the remedy, and the princess was instantly cured. The joyful monarch bestowed upon the hermit his daughter's hand and made him the supreme vizier. When the envious neighbor eventually appeared at court, expecting to be cast into chains, the new vizier recognized him, embraced him, and gifted him a thousand gold pieces and a fertile estate, proving that nobility repays treachery with boundless mercy.
moral: Envy poisons the vessel that contains it, while goodness and forgiveness rise above all attempts to destroy them.

title: The Third Kalandar's Tale
full_text:
The third one-eyed Kalandar stepped forward and said: "My name is Ajib, son of King Hammad. My downfall began when my ship was driven by a violent storm toward the dreaded Loadstone Mountain. The mountain’s magnetic power was so immense that it drew all the iron nails from our vessel, causing the ship to fall to pieces in the roaring waves.

I alone reached the rocky shore. Guided by a dream, I climbed to the summit of the mountain, where stood a bronze dome surmounted by a horseman of brass. Using a magical bow, I shot the talismanic horseman, who fell into the sea, breaking the mountain's enchantment. Immediately, a boat steered by an angel of brass appeared and carried me safely to a paradisiacal island.

There I discovered a subterranean palace where a gentle youth had been hidden by his father to escape an astrological prophecy predicting he would be slain by King Ajib. I befriended the boy, swearing to protect him with my life. But alas! On the very day the prophecy was to expire, as I climbed onto a table to slice a melon for him, my foot slipped, the knife flew from my hand, and it pierced the youth’s breast. Stricken with horror at fulfilling the prophecy by accident, I fled into the forest.

Eventually, I reached a magnificent palace inhabited by forty peerless maidens. They welcomed me as their sovereign, showering me with delights. When they had to depart for forty days on an annual journey, they handed me the keys to a hundred golden doors, saying: 'Enter where you will and feast your eyes on every wonder, but on your life, do not open the golden door of ebony.'

For thirty-nine days I explored thirty-nine rooms filled with gardens, fountains, and jewels. But on the fortieth day, consumed by reckless curiosity, I unlocked the forbidden ebony door. Inside stood a black winged stallion. When I mounted him, the steed leaped into the clouds, flew across continents, and threw me onto a rocky terrace in Baghdad, blinding my left eye with a lash of its tail before vanishing forever. Thus did my unbridled curiosity leave me a blind wanderer in mourning."
moral: Forbidden curiosity and breaking solemn trusts lead to irrevocable loss and long regret.

title: The Eldest Lady's Tale
full_text:
Now it was the turn of the mistress of the mansion, the noble lady Zubaida, to explain the mystery of her home and why she wept over two black hounds every evening.

"Know, O noble assembly," said Zubaida, "that these two black bitches are my own half-sisters. When our father died, leaving us an equal inheritance, my sisters married profligate men who squandered their portions and abandoned them. Twice they returned to me in rags, and twice I clothed them, opened my purse, and shared my wealth without a single word of reproach.

Desiring to increase our fortunes, we purchased a merchant vessel and sailed for distant ports. After weeks of fair winds, we anchored off the coast of a magnificent city whose towers gleamed like silver. But when I went ashore, a chilling sight met my eyes: every inhabitant—the guards at the gate, the merchants in the bazaar, the judges upon their benches, and the king upon his throne—had been turned into solid black stone!

As I explored the silent palaces, I heard a sweet voice reciting verses of devotion. Entering an inner sanctuary, I found the young prince of the city, alive and radiant. He revealed that an ancient curse had petrified his idolatrous people, while he had been preserved because of his adherence to the path of righteousness. We fell deeply in love, and he agreed to sail back with me to Baghdad to become my husband.

When we boarded the ship, my sisters beheld his beauty, royalty, and our shared happiness. Green envy seized their hearts. One stormy night, while the prince and I slept on the deck, my sisters hurled us into the raging waves. The noble prince sank into the deep, but I was cast upon an island. A winged serpent appeared, pursued by a monstrous dragon. I seized a rock and crushed the dragon's head. The serpent transformed into a lovely fairy who, in gratitude for saving her life, carried me back to Baghdad and transformed my treacherous sisters into these two black hounds, bidding me whip them lightly each night as a reminder of their crime, yet care for them with food and shelter.

Though they sought my death, I cannot banish them from my heart. I weep over their transformation and pray daily that the fairy may restore them to human form."
moral: Mercy and compassion toward those who wronged us prove that true nobility cannot be conquered by cruelty.

title: Tale of the Portress
full_text:
Next spoke the gentle portress, the fair Amine, whose scarred shoulders had puzzled the Caliph and his companions all through the evening:

"I too was once the happiest of women, courted by a noble lord of high estate. When we wed, he made but one condition: that I should speak to no other man and ask for no favors outside our household. For months we lived in supreme bliss and tenderness, sharing every joy of heart and mind.

One morning, my elder sister required rare silks for a celebration, and I went to the bazaar accompanied by my elderly maid. We entered the shop of a young merchant famed for the finest Syrian brocades. When I chose the fabric, the merchant refused gold, saying: 'I ask no coin for this silk, but only leave to kiss your cheek through your veil.' I was horrified and turned to leave, but my foolish maid urged me, whispering that it was a trifling matter and that no one would ever know.

Pressed by her persuasion, I turned my cheek slightly through the veil. But the treacherous merchant seized the moment not to kiss me gently, but to bite my cheek so violently that blood stained my veil. Terrified, I fled home and bound my wound with scented bandages.

When my husband returned, he noticed the bandage and asked what had befallen me. In my terror, I lied, claiming that a piece of glass had shattered and grazed my cheek. My husband called for a surgeon, who examined the wound and declared it to be the mark of teeth. My husband's love turned to icy fury. He believed I had betrayed his sacred trust. Summoning his servants, he ordered me to be beaten with willow rods until my shoulders were marked forever, and cast me into the streets.

My noble sister Zubaida took me in, bathed my wounds, and gave me shelter. I bear these scars not as a badge of shame, but as an eternal lesson that a falsehood spoken to shield a minor folly can destroy the greatest palace of love."

Hearing these remarkable tales, Caliph Harun al-Rashid threw off his disguise, summoned his royal power, and reconciled all the ladies, the Kalandars, and the porter, lifting the shadow of enchantment from their lives forever.
moral: Fidelity to sacred promises preserves honor, while jealousy without cause wounds the truest heart.

title: The Tale of the Three Apples
full_text:
One moonless night, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid walked through the streets of Baghdad accompanied by his vizier Ja'afar and Masrur the executioner. Near the Tigris, they encountered an impoverished fisherman weeping over his empty net. The Caliph promised him a hundred gold dinars if he cast his net once more in their name. The fisherman cast, and drew up a heavy wooden chest bound with iron cords.

When Ja'afar broke open the chest, they found inside, wrapped in a costly carpet, the body of a young maiden. Horrified by such an atrocity in his capital, the Caliph turned fiercely upon his vizier: "By the heavens, Ja'afar, if you do not find the murderer of this innocent maiden within three days, you and forty of your kinsmen shall hang upon forty gibbets before my palace gates!"

Ja'afar searched all of Baghdad, but found no trace of the culprit. On the third day, as the gibbets were prepared, a handsome young merchant pushed through the crowd, crying: "I am the murderer, O Commander of the Faithful! Execute me and spare the innocent vizier!" Immediately behind him, an elderly shaykh rushed forward, shouting: "Do not believe him! I alone committed the crime!"

Brought before the Caliph, the young merchant wept and revealed the tragic truth: the maiden was his beloved wife. When she fell ill with a fever, she longed for a single apple. The merchant traveled for weeks all the way to Basra, paying three gold dinars for three rare apples. When he returned, she had already recovered, but could eat only a small morsel.

Walking through the market later that day, the merchant saw a slave holding one of the rare apples. When asked where he obtained it, the slave mocked him: "My mistress gave it to me, boasting that her foolish husband traveled all the way to Basra to fetch it!" Blinded by jealous rage, the merchant rushed home, struck down his innocent wife, and cast her body into the river in a chest. Only when he returned did his little son confess that he had taken the apple to play in the street, where an insolent slave had stolen it from him!

Hearing this heartbreaking tale, the Caliph realized the young husband had acted out of agonizing deception. Instead of vengeance, he commanded Ja'afar to find the lying slave whose slander had caused two lives to perish, proving that careless lies can burn a family to ashes.
moral: Hasty suspicion and slander destroy innocent lives, while justice demands deep inquiry and patient wisdom.

title: Tale of Nur al-Din Ali and his Son
full_text:
In Cairo lived two noble brothers, Shams al-Din and Nur al-Din, who served the Sultan as chief viziers. One evening, as they sat discussing the future, they agreed that when they married, if their wives bore a son and a daughter, the children should be wed to unite their households. But an argument arose over the bride-price, and the proud brothers parted in bitter wrath.

Nur al-Din mounted his horse, rode eastward across the deserts, and settled in the distant city of Basra. There his wisdom won the heart of the local vizier, who gave him his daughter in marriage. In time, Nur al-Din was blessed with a son of peerless beauty named Badr al-Din Hasan, while in Cairo, Shams al-Din had a daughter named Sitt al-Husn.

Years passed, and Nur al-Din died in Basra. His grieving son Badr al-Din fell asleep upon his father's tomb in the cemetery. During the night, two playful spirits beheld the sleeping youth's extraordinary beauty. Knowing that in Cairo the Sultan was forcing Sitt al-Husn to marry an ugly, hunchbacked groom, the spirits lifted Badr al-Din through the air, carried him across hundreds of leagues, and placed him in the bridal chamber of Cairo. When the maiden saw the handsome stranger, she fell instantly in love, and Badr al-Din left with her his purse and his signet ring before falling asleep.

At dawn, before the household awakened, the spirits lifted Badr al-Din again, but a sudden celestial battle forced them to drop him outside the gates of Damascus, clad only in his nightshirt. Bewildered, Badr al-Din took refuge with a kindly pastry-cook, who adopted him and taught him the art of baking exquisite pomegranate-seed tarts.

Ten years later, Shams al-Din, traveling with his daughter and grandson to find his brother's descendants, stopped in Damascus. The young grandson tasted a pomegranate tart from the local shop and exclaimed: "Never have I tasted such tarts save from the hand of my mother!" Shams al-Din examined the recipe, summoned the baker, and matched the signet ring, discovering that the humble pastry-cook was none other than his nephew Badr al-Din Hasan. The brothers' estrangement was healed across generations, and the family was joyfully reunited in Cairo amidst grand celebrations.
moral: Destiny guides separated kin through the most improbable paths, weaving reunion out of small acts of beauty.

title: The Hunchback's Tale
full_text:
In a great city of China, a merry tailor sat working in his shop with his wife. One evening, a comical little hunchback who was the Sultan's favorite court jester stopped before the door, singing whimsical songs and beating a small tambourine. Delighted by his merriment, the tailor invited him home for supper, serving a bowl of fried fish.

As the hunchback swallowed a large morsel of fish, a sharp bone lodged in his throat. He choked, rolled his eyes, and collapsed motionless onto the floor. The tailor and his wife were seized with panic, crying: "Woe unto us! If the Sultan discovers his jester dead in our house, we shall all be hanged!"

Under cover of darkness, they carried the body to the house of a Jewish physician, pushed it past the entryway stairs, and fled. The physician, descending the dark stairs in haste, accidentally kicked the body, sending it tumbling to the bottom. Believing he had killed a patient, the terrified doctor lowered the corpse down the chimney into his neighbor's courtyard—the kitchen of the Sultan's chief steward.

When the steward entered and saw a dark figure standing near his oil jars, he thought it was a thief and struck it with a heavy cudgel. The body fell limp. Horrified that he had slain a man, the steward propped the corpse against a shopfront in the bazaar. A tipsy foreign broker, walking past, bumped into the hunchback and, thinking he was being assaulted, struck him with his fist. The night watchman arrived at that very moment, seized the broker, and dragged him to the gallows for murder!

Just as the noose was placed around the broker's neck, the steward rushed forward, shouting: "Hang me! I killed him!" Then the physician arrived, crying: "No, I killed him!" Finally the tailor ran up, confessing: "It was my fish bone that choked him!"

The Sultan, hearing of this astonishing chain of confessions, summoned all four men to court, laughing at their comical panic. A clever barber stepped forward, reached into the hunchback's throat with delicate pincers, and drew out the fish bone. The hunchback sneezed, opened his eyes, and leaped to his feet! The Sultan pardoned everyone, rewarded their honesty, and made the evening an occasion of royal celebration.
moral: Panic and fear of the law make honest men look guilty, but truth and calm investigation reveal innocence.

title: The Nazarene Broker's Story
full_text:
To entertain the Sultan of China, the Christian broker recounted his own remarkable adventure when he was a young merchant in Damascus:

"In my youth, I traded in fine Egyptian linens and Persian silks. One day, a young Syrian gentleman of striking beauty and refined manners entered my warehouse. He offered to sell me fifty bundles of rare damask on credit, agreeing to collect the payment in installments. I sold the goods at a handsome profit, but when the youth returned to collect his gold, he took only a small handful, leaving the rest in my vault, saying: 'Keep it safe, brother, until I have need of it.'

This continued for many months. The youth’s trust and modesty won my deepest admiration. One evening, he invited me to a lavish feast at a garden palace outside Damascus. There, surrounded by fountains and singing lutes, he recounted how he had once been a foolish youth who squandered his inheritance in Cairo through reckless indulgence.

He had fallen under the spell of extravagant companions who urged him to buy gems, perfumes, and banquets beyond his means. When his fortune evaporated, his false friends vanished like shadows, leaving him without a crust of bread. In his desperation, he had learned the bitter value of labor, taking service as a simple caravan driver across the Syrian desert.

'Through hardship, heat, and sandstorms,' said the youth, 'I discovered that wealth easily gained is easily lost, but a single dirham earned by sweat carries a blessing that multiplies.' He had invested his modest wages in the silk trade, swearing an oath to practice moderation, keep his promises, and trust only those who demonstrated integrity in small things.

I listened to his tale with profound reverence, realizing that the young man’s true treasure was not the gold in my vault, but the golden wisdom he had forged in the crucible of adversity. We remained partners and steadfast friends for thirty years, proving that true wealth is measured not by what one spends, but by the dignity with which one lives."
moral: Frugality, self-restraint, and honest commerce protect a youth from the perils of extravagance.

title: The Reeve's Tale
full_text:
The Sultan’s steward, having been pardoned by his monarch, then related his own curious history to explain why he never partook of dishes seasoned with cumin and garlic without first washing his hands forty times:

"When I was a young man in Baghdad, I fell in love with a noble maiden of the high court. Her mother consented to our union on one solemn condition: that I must swear never to eat a seasoned meat dish without thoroughly washing my hands with scented potash, dried lupin flour, and rosewater, out of respect for the refinement of her ancestral home.

In the first joy of youth, I took the vow lightly, thinking it a trivial matter of courtly manners. For years I kept the custom faithfully. But one day, after a long journey in the heat of summer, I stopped at a roadside tavern where a cook was frying savory minced meat heavily spiced with garlic, cumin, and coriander. Starving and exhausted, I devoured the dish greedily and wiped my fingers carelessly upon my sleeve, forgetting my sacred pledge.

When I returned to my wife's presence, the pungent scent betrayed my neglect. My wife turned pale with sorrow and said: 'He who breaks a solemn pledge in a small matter will surely fail when tested by great honor.' She refused to sit beside me and retreated to her chamber, leaving me to reflect in solitude on the sanctity of promises.

Stung by conscience, I realized the profound truth of her words. A vow is not measured by the size of the deed, but by the integrity of the soul that utters it. I went to the fountain, washed my hands forty times with soap, ash, and rosewater, and bowed before her door, seeking forgiveness with genuine remorse.

Seeing my repentance, my wife opened her door and smiled: 'It was not the garlic that grieved me, but the fragility of your word. Now that you understand that honor dwells in every breath and gesture, we are truly one.' From that day forth, I have never touched seasoned food without the forty ritual washings, honoring the memory of the lesson that preserved our household."
moral: Respect for sacred vows and keeping one's word in all matters builds a character of lasting honor.

title: Tale of the Jewish Doctor
full_text:
To entertain the Sultan of China and clear his own name in the strange affair of the hunchback, the Jewish physician related a mystery from his youth in Damascus:

"In my early years of practice, I was summoned in haste to the palace of the city governor to treat a young merchant of Baghdad who had fallen into a deep swoon. When I loosened his garments, I discovered that his right wrist had been severed and wrapped in scented silk bandages. After reviving him with cordials and smelling salts, I sat beside his couch, struck by his noble countenance and sorrowful eyes.

Seeing my genuine concern, the young merchant wept and confided his secret: 'Know, O doctor, that I was once wealthy, inheriting a grand silk emporium. While trading in Damascus, a veiled lady of matchless beauty entered my shop, purchasing costly brocades on credit. For weeks she returned, always paying with purest gold dinars and speaking with refined grace. My heart became deeply attached to her virtues.'

One evening, she invited him to her family's garden mansion. As they sat dining beneath jasmine arbors, a precious golden necklace belonging to the governor's household went missing from the terrace. The household guards surrounded the garden, and in the confusion, the young merchant, wishing to shield the maiden from disgrace, placed the jewel in his own pocket, intending to return it to the governor at dawn.

The guards searched him, discovered the necklace, and dragged him before the magistrate as a thief. The harsh magistrate ordered his hand severed according to the strict law of the city. Only later did the governor's wife confess that her pet monkey had snatched the necklace and dropped it upon the garden path.

The remorseful governor bestowed palaces, wealth, and the maiden's hand upon the noble youth to atone for the error. 'I bear this severed hand,' concluded the merchant, 'as a testament to the peril of hasty judgment.' I attended to his wound with all my skill, marveling at how noble souls bear adversity with silent dignity."
moral: Honest compassion and professional duty bridge all divides, while hasty suspicion brings regret.

title: Tale of the Tailor
full_text:
The tailor of China then related the story of a lame young man from Baghdad who had fled his own wedding feast because of an intolerable barber:

"Yesterday, I attended a banquet in our city given by a wealthy youth of Baghdad. When the guests were seated and the roasted meats served, a handsome young merchant entered, limping heavily. The moment his eyes fell upon an elderly, talkative barber who sat among the guests, the youth turned pale, leaped to his feet, and cried: 'I must depart! Either this babbler leaves this room, or I must wander into the desert!'

The astonished host begged the youth to explain his strange wrath. The lame merchant sighed and recounted his misadventure:

'In Baghdad, I was once courted by the daughter of the chief judge. On the day of our betrothal, I summoned a barber to trim my hair and prepare my attire for the wedding ceremony. Instead of sharpening his razors and performing his task, the barber produced an astrolabe, measured the altitude of the sun, and began reciting astrological charts! He babbled endlessly about planetary alignments, the history of his seven brothers, and his own incomparable wisdom in philosophy, grammar, and divination.

For three mortal hours I begged him to make haste, for the hour of the ceremony was fast approaching. Yet every time he touched his shears to my head, he paused to deliver a sermon on humility or to recount a lengthy anecdote of his childhood. Driven to distraction, I shouted at him to finish. Offended by my impatience, he insisted on accompanying me to the bride's house to protect me from evil stars!

When I reached the judge's courtyard, the barber stood outside shouting comical predictions and causing such an uproar that the neighbors believed a riot had broken out. In trying to escape his ceaseless chatter, I jumped from a first-floor window into the street, shattering my ankle and becoming lame for life. From that hour, I swore never to dwell in the same city as that unbridled tongue!'

Hearing this, all the guests turned and glared at the barber, who merely shook his head and claimed that his only flaw was an excess of benevolence!"
moral: A busybody who speaks without restraint can ruin the happiest gatherings and drive away peace.

title: The Barber's Tale of Himself
full_text:
The barber, seeing the company amused yet critical of his reputation, stroked his long white beard and spoke with supreme vanity before the Sultan:

"Know, O Sovereign of China, that men call me Al-Samit, which means the Silent, because of my famous taciturnity and restraint in speech! I am the fifth son of a venerable sage, and my six brothers were each afflicted with some peculiar defect, whereas I alone was born perfect in mind, body, and eloquence. I am a master of astrology, medicine, alchemy, logic, and the subtle art of the blade.

In the reign of the Caliph Al-Mustansir in Baghdad, ten notorious river pirates were captured upon the Tigris and condemned to be transported downriver for exile. As they were being marched to the barge in chains, I saw the procession passing through the market. Moved by tender sympathy and believing they were honest scholars being honored with royal gifts, I quietly slipped into their ranks, joined hands with them, and boarded the ship!

When the captain examined his prisoners on the far shore, he counted ten felons and myself as an extra passenger. Without inquiring into my name or character, the rough boatmen assumed I was the ringleader of the band! When the executioner raised his staff to chastise us, the ten pirates confessed their crimes, but I, preserving my celebrated vow of silence, merely smiled with philosophical serenity, believing that my noble countenance would speak for itself.

Fortunately, the Caliph’s grand vizier arrived at the docks to inspect the prisoners. Recognizing my famous face, he shouted: 'Hold your hand! That is the silent barber of Baghdad, whose tongue is more plentiful than the sands of the desert! How came you among these ruffians, O barber?'

I stepped forward and delivered an eloquent oration of two hours, explaining the astronomical configurations of the moon and the moral virtues of fraternal solidarity. The vizier laughed until he fell backward, pardoned me on the condition that I hold my peace for one whole day, and sent me home with fifty dinars. Thus you see, O king, that my only fault is that my heart is too vast for this narrow world!"
moral: Self-praise and uninvited meddling turn well-intentioned advice into an intolerable nuisance.

title: The Barber's Tale of his First Brother
full_text:
To prove that his brothers were far more unfortunate than he, the barber recounted the history of his eldest brother, Al-Baqbuq the Hunchback:

"My brother Al-Baqbuq was an industrious weaver who lived in Baghdad, earning a quiet living at his handloom. His workshop stood adjacent to the grand mansion of an affluent flour merchant whose garden overlooked my brother's small courtyard. One afternoon, Al-Baqbuq looked through his window and saw the merchant's daughter watering jasmine plants on the upper terrace. Struck by her grace, he sighed and neglected his loom.

The flour merchant’s cunning steward noticed the weaver’s infatuation and resolved to exploit it for his master’s profit. The steward approached Al-Baqbuq and whispered: 'The young lady has observed your noble industry and wishes to reward you. If you will bring your finest rolls of woven damask to our mill tonight, she will purchase them at thrice their market value and grant you her favor.'

Overjoyed by this prospect, Al-Baqbuq gathered all his woven cloth and carried it to the mill after dark. But instead of the maiden, the mischievous steward met him with heavy sacks of grain. 'Before the lady arrives,' said the steward, 'prove your manly strength by turning the water-wheel, for the mule is weary.' The gullible hunchback pushed the heavy wooden millstone for hours until his arms burned and his breath failed.

At midnight, the steward returned with the flour merchant, shouting that a thief had broken into the mill to steal flour! The merchant beat poor Al-Baqbuq with an olive cudgel, stripped him of his fine damask, and drove him naked into the street. The wretched weaver returned to his empty loom, learning that false promises are nothing but chaff before the wind, and that he who chases vanity loses both his cloth and his dignity."
moral: Patience and honest labor are safer guides than foolish greed and deceptive neighbors.

title: The Barber's Tale of his Second Brother
full_text:
The barber continued his chronicle, recounting the misadventure of his second brother, Al-Haddar:

"My brother Al-Haddar was a man endowed with great physical stature, but his mind was so clouded by vanity that he believed every maiden in Baghdad was secretly enamored of his beauty. One sunny morning, as he sat before his house perfuming his beard, an elderly woman stopped before him and sighed: 'Alas, what a peerless youth! A noble lady of royal blood has seen you from her balcony and is dying of love. If you possess the courage to visit her palace, untold riches and bliss await you.'

Al-Haddar’s chest swelled with pride. He donned his finest embroidered vest and followed the old woman through winding alleys to a magnificent palace. Ushered into an inner salon filled with marble basins and silk cushions, he was greeted by four mischievous maidens who claimed to be the attendants of the princess.

'Before you may sit upon the sofa of honor,' said the elder maid with suppressed laughter, 'it is the custom of our palace that every suitor must prove his playfulness. You must allow us to shave your eyebrows, dye your cheeks with yellow saffron, and dance with a tambourine!'

Blind to the ridicule, Al-Haddar submitted meekly. The maidens shaved his thick eyebrows, painted his face like a carnival clown, placed a dunce's cap upon his crown, and made him dance in circles while they clapped their hands. Then, promising that the princess was waiting behind the garden gate, they pushed him through a curtained doorway.

The door snapped shut behind him, and Al-Haddar found himself tumbling through a dark laundry chute, landing directly in the middle of the crowded leather-tanners’ bazaar! When the tanners saw a monstrous figure with a yellow face, shaved brows, and a conical cap leaping out of the wall, they took him for an evil goblin and beat him with wet hides until he fled the quarter. Thus did my brother learn that vanity turns a man into a laughingstock for the amusement of others."
moral: Vanity makes a fool blind to the most obvious traps laid by deceitful flatterers.
